entries.name: select_field_of_nested_tuple-accept#0
entries.script: [P1] `SizeOf(SelectField(((1,2,3), 4), 1))` — **3 at cost 29.** The first route: a non-pair tuple nested inside a PAIR, pulled out by `SelectField`. `checkType` is shallow, so the outer pair's field access never inspects the inner tuple's arity. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: select_field_of_nested_coll_control-accept#1
entries.script: [C1] **CONTROL for P1** — the same shape with a `Coll[Int]` in the field instead of a tuple: 3 at cost 49. Dearer than P1 by 20 because the field is built by a `Tuple` NODE here rather than read out of a constant, which is what shows P1's cost belongs to the constant.

entries.name: item_of_data_collection-accept#2
entries.script: [P2] `SizeOf(ByIndex(Coll((1,2,3)), 0))` — **3 at cost 54.** The second route: an ITEM of a data collection of tuples. The item's runtime type is `Coll[Any]`, so `SizeOf` reads it. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: content_of_an_option-accept#3
entries.script: [P3] `SizeOf(OptionGet(Some((1,2,3))))` — **3 at cost 34.** The third route. Note the v0 twin of this row does not exist: `SOption` data requires ErgoTree v3, and an unsized tree has no size bit to degrade behind, so the v0 form is REJECTED outright. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: deserialize_to_tuple-accept#4
entries.script: [P4] `SizeOf(Global.deserializeTo[(Int,Int,Int)](020406))` — **3 at cost 160**, the dearest route and the fourth: the value is built by the DATA deserializer at eval time from three bytes, which is the path `CoreDataSerializer` takes on a register or an extension. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: data_collection_root-accept#5
entries.script: [P5] `Coll((1,2,3))` as the ROOT — **cost 5**, and the row to read for its VALUE rather than its cost: `{"kind":"Coll","elem":{"tag":"SColl","elem":{"tag":"SAny"}},…}` with each item a `Coll[SAny]`. A data collection of non-pair tuples carries `tItem = collRType(AnyType)` and NOT the tuple type, so this is the second place the corpus writes `{"tag":"SAny"}` (the first being `Tuple.non_pair_value_ops` T5). **SEPARATING:** an implementation that keeps the tuple type as the item type writes a different `elem` here and is red for the encoding. All three conformers with an eval arm do exactly that. **And the item type IS observable to a script, through a second producer** — a collection EXPRESSION in a register carries the TUPLE type, so it compares `false` against this data form where another data collection compares `true`; see the family header, which corrects an earlier claim of mine that it could not be seen.

entries.name: eq_two_data_collections-accept#6
entries.script: [E1] `Coll((1,2,3)) == Coll((1,2,3))` — **true at cost 49.** `DataValueComparer` compares item types before any item, and two data collections of non-pair tuples share `Coll[Any]`, so they compare equal. **SEPARATING, and the round's one COST divergence:** sigma-rust answers `true` at 36 — correct value, 13 low — and the same 13 on E2 and E3, so it is one number.

entries.name: eq_two_coll_of_coll_control-accept#7
entries.script: [C2] **CONTROL for E1** — `Coll(Coll[Int](1,2,3)) == Coll(Coll[Int](1,2,3))`, the same nesting with a declared item type: true at cost 41. The 8 between them is the tuple collection's own encoding, not a different comparison. (This cross pair — a tuple collection against THIS one — cannot be written: the operands' static types disagree and the builder's SameType check refuses it at PARSE. That does NOT make the item type unobservable: two collections of the same declared type and different item types are writable, and they separate — see the family header.)

entries.name: eq_two_options-accept#8
entries.script: [E2] `Some((1,2,3)) == Some((1,2,3))` — **true at cost 40.** Scala's `==` reaches inside the `Option` and then compares two `Coll[Any]`s. **SEPARATING** (sigma-rust: 27, the same 13).

entries.name: eq_two_pairs_holding_tuples-accept#9
entries.script: [E3] `((1,2,3), 4) == ((1,2,3), 4)` — **true at cost 43**, the third container. **SEPARATING** (sigma-rust: 30, the same 13). The three E rows together say the undercharge is in the tuple's own comparison and not in any one container.
